def: An atypical antipsychotic that acts as a partial agonist at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT1A receptors. Used for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder; less weight gain and prolactin elevation than other atypicals.
A dissociative anesthetic drug of abuse that blocks NMDA glutamate receptors. Intoxication causes agitation, violent behavior, nystagmus and hallucinations. Similar in action to ketamine.
The odds of exposure in cases divided by the odds of exposure in controls. It is the measure of association in case-control studies and approximates relative risk when the disease is rare.
CD8-positive T lymphocytes that recognize antigen on MHC class I and kill infected or tumor cells by releasing perforin and granzymes, which trigger apoptosis.
A protein on activated helper T cells that binds CD40 on B cells to drive isotype class switching. Defective in X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome.
The arm of adaptive immunity carried out by antibodies secreted by B cells and plasma cells, mainly defending against extracellular microbes and toxins.
A live attenuated vaccine against varicella-zoster virus, given in two doses in childhood. Contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency.
A vaccine made of purified viral or bacterial components (such as a surface protein) instead of the whole organism, so it cannot cause infection. Examples are hepatitis B and HPV vaccines.

A systemic illness caused by Salmonella typhi, spread by contaminated food and water. Features sustained fever, rose spots, relative bradycardia and bowel perforation; carriers harbor bacteria in the gallbladder.
Inflammation of skeletal muscle causing proximal weakness and elevated creatine kinase. Includes polymyositis, dermatomyositis and inclusion body myositis.
An immunodeficiency, often from CD40 ligand defects, where B cells cannot class switch. Patients have high IgM but low IgG, IgA and IgE and suffer recurrent bacterial infections.
An X-linked immunodeficiency from a WAS gene mutation causing the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections.
Autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I). They cause venous and arterial clots and pregnancy loss, and prolong the aPTT.
An enzyme that relieves DNA supercoiling by making single-strand breaks. Inhibited by irinotecan and topotecan; autoantibodies to it occur in diffuse systemic sclerosis.
A small benign bone-forming tumor with a central nidus, most often in the long bones of young people. Causes night pain that is relieved by NSAIDs.
A malignant cartilage-producing tumor of the pelvis, femur and shoulder in middle-aged adults. Histology shows atypical chondrocytes in a cartilage matrix; it resists chemotherapy.
A group of HLA-B27-associated inflammatory arthritides involving the spine and sacroiliac joints, without rheumatoid factor. Includes ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic and reactive arthritis.
A large cytoskeletal protein that links the muscle cell membrane to actin. Absent in Duchenne and defective in Becker muscular dystrophy (X-linked).
A rough, scaly precancerous skin patch on sun-exposed skin caused by UV damage. It can progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
Widespread skin blistering and peeling caused by Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxins that cleave desmoglein-1. Seen in infants and children; positive Nikolsky sign, with mucosa spared.
A synthetic anticoagulant that indirectly inhibits factor Xa by binding antithrombin. Given subcutaneously; does not cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia but is cleared by the kidney.
A broad-spectrum combination of an extended-spectrum penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor. Covers Pseudomonas, anaerobes and many gram-negative rods.
A fifth-generation cephalosporin that binds PBP2a, so it is active against MRSA and many gram-negative bacteria. Not active against Pseudomonas.

term: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma
def: A rapid bedside ultrasound of the pericardium, hepatorenal pouch, splenorenal space and pelvis looking for free fluid in blunt abdominal trauma.
Surgical removal of lymph nodes, done to stage or treat cancer. A complication is lymphedema in the drained region.
Impaired bile flow arising within the liver, producing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, itching and raised alkaline phosphatase. Seen with drugs, pregnancy and primary biliary cholangitis.
Vitamin A derivatives that bind nuclear retinoic acid receptors. Used for acne (isotretinoin) and leukemia (tretinoin); they are strongly teratogenic.
A monoclonal antibody against HER2/neu used for HER2-positive breast and gastric cancer. Its main toxicity is cardiomyopathy.
Chemotherapy drugs (paclitaxel, docetaxel) that stabilize microtubules and block mitosis in M phase. Toxicities include neutropenia and peripheral neuropathy.
A respiratory fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Covers anaerobes and atypicals; risks are tendon rupture and QT prolongation.
The diamond-shaped region between the pubic symphysis and coccyx, containing the urogenital and anal triangles that hold the external genitalia and anus.
Infection with Entamoeba histolytica, acquired by fecal-oral cyst ingestion. Causes bloody dysentery and liver abscesses; treated with metronidazole.
An aminoglycoside that is not absorbed from the gut. Used to treat intestinal amebiasis and Cryptosporidium and Giardia in pregnancy.
Single-celled fungi, such as Saccharomyces and Candida, that reproduce by forming daughter buds from the parent cell.
Louse-borne illness caused by Rickettsia prowazekii. Causes fever and a rash that begins on the trunk and spreads outward, sparing palms and soles.
An echinocandin antifungal that inhibits beta-glucan synthesis in the fungal cell wall. Active against Candida and Aspergillus; given IV.
A polypeptide antibiotic that blocks bacterial cell wall synthesis. Used topically because it is nephrotoxic systemically.
A sexually transmitted infection caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, producing a painful genital ulcer with tender inguinal lymph nodes.
Syphilis passed across the placenta to the fetus. Signs include saddle nose, Hutchinson teeth, mulberry molars, saber shins and sensorineural deafness.
A spirochete infection (Leptospira) from water contaminated by animal urine. Severe form (Weil disease) causes jaundice, kidney failure and bleeding.
A complete, infectious viral particle outside a host cell, consisting of nucleic acid in a protein capsid, sometimes with an envelope.
A herpesvirus of macaque monkeys (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1) that can cause fatal encephalitis in humans after bites or scratches.
A partially double-stranded DNA virus of the Hepadnaviridae that replicates through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase. Causes acute and chronic hepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abnormal staining masses inside infected cell nuclei. Examples are Cowdry type A inclusions in herpesviruses and owl's-eye inclusions in CMV.
Sexually transmitted infection with HSV-2 (sometimes HSV-1) causing painful vesicles and ulcers. The virus stays latent in sacral ganglia.
A marine gram-negative bacterium causing wound infection and septicemia after raw oyster consumption, with hemorrhagic bullous skin lesions, especially in patients with liver disease.
Brain infection with larval Taenia solium cysts, from ingesting eggs. Leading cause of adult-onset seizures worldwide; CT shows cystic lesions with a scolex.
Pain radiating down the back of the leg along the sciatic nerve, usually from lumbar disc herniation compressing the L5 or S1 root.
A pus collection in the epidural space, usually from Staphylococcus aureus. Causes back pain, fever and progressive neurologic deficits from cord compression.
Overgrowth of anaerobes such as Gardnerella with loss of lactobacilli. Gives a thin gray discharge, fishy odor, pH above 4.5 and clue cells.
Infection of the mediastinum, often after esophageal rupture or cardiac surgery. Presents with chest pain, fever and sepsis.
Folinic acid, a reduced folate that bypasses dihydrofolate reductase. Used to rescue normal cells from methotrexate toxicity and to enhance 5-fluorouracil.
Narrowing of the spinal canal that compresses nerves, causing neurogenic claudication: leg pain on walking that improves when bending forward.
Anti-D antibody given to Rh-negative mothers around delivery or bleeding to prevent sensitization and hemolytic disease in later Rh-positive fetuses.
Enveloped positive-sense RNA viruses with icosahedral capsids. Include rubella virus and alphaviruses such as eastern equine encephalitis and chikungunya.
Widespread shearing of axons from rotational acceleration-deceleration head trauma, with coma and punctate hemorrhages at the gray-white junction.

A small non-enveloped DNA virus family. JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, BK virus causes kidney transplant nephropathy, and Merkel cell polyomavirus causes Merkel cell carcinoma.
A low-risk HPV type that causes genital warts (condylomata acuminata), along with type 11.
A polymyxin antibiotic that disrupts the gram-negative outer membrane. Reserved for multidrug-resistant bacteria; toxic to kidneys and nerves.
A gram-positive coccus often resistant to vancomycin (VRE) and ampicillin, a common cause of hospital-acquired infections.
Formerly Streptococcus bovis, a group D strep that causes endocarditis and is associated with colon cancer.
Direct visualization of the bladder and urethra through an endoscope, used to find bladder tumors, stones and sources of hematuria.
An oral prodrug of penciclovir that inhibits viral DNA polymerase after activation by viral thymidine kinase. Treats herpes simplex and zoster.
An abnormal layer of inflamed granulation tissue that overgrows joint cartilage in rheumatoid arthritis, destroying cartilage and bone.
A first-generation H1 antihistamine that crosses into the brain, causing sedation and anticholinergic effects. Used for allergy and as a sleep aid.
An H2 receptor blocker that reduces gastric acid. It inhibits cytochrome P450 and has antiandrogen effects such as gynecomastia.
A nonabsorbable sugar that is fermented by gut bacteria. Used to treat constipation and hepatic encephalopathy by trapping ammonia as ammonium.
An enzyme that cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG. It acts as the second messenger system of Gq-coupled receptors.
A small intracellular molecule, such as cAMP, cGMP, IP3, DAG or calcium, that relays a receptor signal from the cell surface to targets inside the cell.
Elevated pressure in the pulmonary arteries from narrowing of small pulmonary vessels. Causes dyspnea and right heart failure; treated with endothelin antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors and prostacyclins.
A polar amino acid with a hydroxyl group. A common site of phosphorylation and a precursor to glycine and cysteine.
Excess growth hormone before epiphyseal closure, usually from a pituitary adenoma, causing abnormally tall stature. After closure the same excess causes acromegaly.
Movement of organelles and proteins along microtubules in a neuron. Kinesin moves cargo anterograde, dynein retrograde; used by rabies and herpes viruses to reach the cell body.
IgG autoantibodies that bind and activate the TSH receptor, causing hyperthyroidism in Graves disease.
The innermost layer of the adrenal cortex, which produces adrenal androgens such as DHEA under ACTH control.
A glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid precursor in the adrenal cortex, the intermediate leading to aldosterone.
A steroid enzyme (CYP17A1) with 17-alpha-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase activity needed to make cortisol and sex steroids. Deficiency causes hypertension with hypogonadism.
An enzyme that releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, starting eicosanoid synthesis. Inhibited by corticosteroids via lipocortin.
Islet cells that secrete somatostatin, which inhibits insulin, glucagon and growth hormone release.
Irreversible liver fibrosis with regenerative nodules and distorted architecture. Leads to portal hypertension, ascites and liver failure; common causes are alcohol and viral hepatitis.
Resistance to parathyroid hormone from a GNAS mutation, causing low calcium and high PTH. Albright hereditary osteodystrophy adds short stature and short fourth metacarpals.
The crossing point of the optic nerves where nasal retinal fibers decussate. Lesions here, such as pituitary tumors, cause bitemporal hemianopia.
Herniation of the arachnoid into the sella turcica that flattens the pituitary against its floor, often causing mild pituitary hormone deficits.
The active form of prednisone, an intermediate-acting glucocorticoid used for inflammation and immunosuppression.
A breakdown product of epinephrine made by COMT. Elevated plasma or urine metanephrines are used to diagnose pheochromocytoma.
A rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor of delta cells causing diabetes, gallstones and steatorrhea from inhibition of insulin, cholecystokinin and pancreatic enzymes.
A neuropeptide that relaxes smooth muscle and stimulates intestinal secretion. Excess from a VIPoma causes watery diarrhea with low potassium.
A RET-mutation syndrome with medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus.
A tumor of hormone-producing neuroendocrine cells, such as carcinoid, insulinoma or gastrinoma. Stain positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin.
An enzyme that cleaves glucose units from carbohydrates. Alpha-glucosidase in the gut brush border is blocked by acarbose; lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase is deficient in Pompe disease.
The single cell layer lining blood vessels. It regulates tone via nitric oxide, controls permeability and prevents clotting.
Thickened, leathery, itchy skin with exaggerated markings from chronic rubbing or scratching.
Drugs that act as estrogen agonists in some tissues and antagonists in others. Tamoxifen and raloxifene are examples.
A SERM that acts as an estrogen agonist in bone and antagonist in breast and uterus. Used for osteoporosis; raises risk of venous clots.
A SERM that blocks estrogen feedback at the hypothalamus, raising GnRH, FSH and LH. Used to induce ovulation.
A malignant tumor of smooth muscle, most often in the uterus, retroperitoneum or gut. Unlike benign leiomyomas it shows atypia, necrosis and mitoses.
A malignant glandular tumor forming cystic spaces, most often in the ovary or pancreas.
A protein made by the fetal liver and yolk sac. Raised in neural tube defects and abdominal wall defects; also a tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac tumors.
A yellow carotenoid pigment concentrated in the macula of the retina. Dietary lutein may lower the risk of age-related macular degeneration.
A cord running through the inguinal canal that carries the vas deferens, testicular vessels, nerves and lymphatics to the testis.
Fluid accumulated in the peritoneal cavity. A serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 or more indicates portal hypertension.
Fibroblasts with smooth muscle features that contract wounds and lay down collagen during healing and fibrosis.
Abnormal dilation of a hollow structure such as a vessel or duct.
Lipid-laden macrophages with a foamy cytoplasm. Characteristic of atherosclerotic plaques, xanthomas and some storage diseases.
The outer fetal membrane that forms the fetal portion of the placenta. Chorionic villi arise from it.
The embryonic remnant of the allantois connecting bladder to umbilicus. Persistence causes a urachal fistula or cyst; it becomes the median umbilical ligament.
An abnormal chromosome number that is not a multiple of the haploid set, such as trisomy 21 or monosomy X. Usually from nondisjunction.
A monoclonal antibody against RANKL that blocks osteoclast formation. Used for osteoporosis and bone metastases; can cause hypocalcemia.
An enzyme that converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxane. Inhibited by NSAIDs and aspirin; COX-2 is selectively blocked by celecoxib.
Pregnancy at age 35 or older, which increases the risk of chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 21.
Fetal vessels running unprotected over the cervical os. Rupture of membranes causes painless bleeding and rapid fetal exsanguination.
The basic unit of chromatin: about 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around a core of eight histones (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4).
Tightly condensed, transcriptionally inactive chromatin that stains dark on electron microscopy. Heavily methylated and deacetylated.
An enzyme that makes double-strand DNA breaks to relieve supercoiling. Targeted by etoposide, doxorubicin, and fluoroquinolones in bacteria.
A bacterial gene cluster for lactose metabolism. It is switched on when lactose is present and glucose is low, via the repressor and cAMP-CAP.
An autosomal recessive defect in nucleotide excision repair causing extreme sun sensitivity and a very high risk of skin cancers.
Error-free repair of DNA double-strand breaks using a sister chromatid as template. Requires BRCA1 and BRCA2.
An inherited DNA crosslink repair defect causing pancytopenia, short stature, radial or thumb anomalies and risk of leukemia.
Genes with a conserved DNA-binding sequence that control body segment identity along the head-to-tail axis. Hox mutations cause limb and organ patterning defects.
Processing of one pre-mRNA into different mature mRNAs by including or skipping exons, allowing one gene to produce several proteins.
The first gap phase of the cell cycle, when the cell grows and prepares for DNA synthesis. Passage through the G1/S checkpoint is controlled by Rb and p53.
The microtubule array that separates chromosomes during cell division. Blocked by vinca alkaloids and taxanes.
Reticular collagen found in skin, vessels, uterus and granulation tissue. Defective in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
An inherited type IV collagen defect causing hematuria with kidney failure, sensorineural hearing loss and eye problems. Basement membrane shows a basket-weave pattern.
A cyclic amino acid that breaks alpha helices. Hydroxylated in collagen by a vitamin C-dependent enzyme.
Scurvy: impaired collagen hydroxylation causing bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, poor wound healing and corkscrew hairs.
An X-linked copper transport (ATP7A) defect causing kinky hair, hypotonia and neurodegeneration from poor lysyl oxidase activity.
An enzyme that breaks down collagen, needed for tissue remodeling. Excess matrix metalloproteinase activity contributes to emphysema and tumor spread.
Random silencing of one X chromosome in each female cell, forming a Barr body. Mediated by XIST RNA.
A childhood eye tumor from loss of both RB1 alleles, presenting with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex). Hereditary form raises risk of osteosarcoma.
Abnormally increased food intake, as in hypothalamic damage, diabetes or Prader-Willi syndrome.
A GNAS mosaic mutation causing polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, cafe-au-lait spots and endocrine hyperfunction such as precocious puberty.
Partial displacement of the lens, seen in Marfan syndrome (upward) and homocystinuria (downward).
Chemoreceptors near the aortic arch that sense low oxygen, high CO2 and low pH. Afferents travel via the vagus nerve.
Buerger disease: inflammation and clotting of small and medium limb vessels in heavy smokers, causing claudication, ulcers and gangrene.
Tear of the aorta, from dissection, aneurysm or trauma at the ligamentum arteriosum. Causes severe pain and a widened mediastinum.
Transient narrowing of a coronary artery causing Prinzmetal angina with ST elevation at rest. Treated with calcium channel blockers and nitrates.
Pressure in the vena cava near the right atrium, reflecting right heart filling and volume status.
Defects from prenatal alcohol exposure: growth restriction, microcephaly, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures and cognitive impairment.
Failure of the fetal opening between the atria to close. Can allow paradoxical embolism from veins to the systemic circulation.
A congenital defect where a single arterial trunk exits both ventricles, from failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to form. Causes cyanosis and heart failure.
Bleeding within the brain tissue, most often from chronic hypertension affecting small vessels of the basal ganglia.
Resistance of Staphylococcus aureus to beta-lactams via the altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a encoded by mecA.
Elevated systolic pressure (above 140) with normal diastolic pressure, from stiff arteries in the elderly.
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, from weak ventricular contraction. Causes include ischemia and dilated cardiomyopathy.
Recycling of bile acids and some drugs from the liver to gut and back via the portal vein. Interrupted by cholestyramine.
Elevated blood triglycerides. Very high levels cause acute pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas and lipemia retinalis.
Hemoglobin with iron in the ferric (Fe3+) state, unable to carry oxygen. Causes chocolate-colored blood and cyanosis; treated with methylene blue.
Attaching ubiquitin to a protein, marking it for degradation by the proteasome.
Drugs such as acetazolamide that block carbonic anhydrase, causing bicarbonate diuresis and metabolic acidosis. Used for glaucoma and altitude sickness.
A benign tumor of blood vessels and fibrous tissue. Seen on the face in tuberous sclerosis and in the nasopharynx of adolescent males.
Fluid in the middle ear without acute infection, causing conductive hearing loss. Common in children with eustachian tube dysfunction.
Anaerobic gram-negative rods of the mouth. Cause Lemierre syndrome (jugular vein thrombophlebitis) and abscesses.
A cytokine made by Th2 cells that promotes eosinophil growth and B-cell class switching to IgA.
A hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus in asthma or cystic fibrosis, with wheeze, brown mucus plugs, high IgE and central bronchiectasis.
Lung disease from inhaled coal dust, producing anthracotic macrophages and nodules. Can progress to massive fibrosis.
Sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia and DIC around labor, as amniotic material enters maternal circulation.
Abnormal retinal vessel growth in preterm infants given oxygen, which can cause retinal detachment and blindness.
Compression of the brachial plexus or subclavian vessels between clavicle and first rib, causing arm pain, numbness or swelling.
A platelet eicosanoid that causes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction. Blocked by low-dose aspirin.
A class of eicosanoids made by COX and thromboxane synthase that promote platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.
AML subtype with t(15;17) producing PML-RARA fusion. Presents with DIC; Auer rods; treated with all-trans retinoic acid.
A bifunctional enzyme controlling fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, which regulates glycolysis versus gluconeogenesis. Insulin activates it in the fed state.
Glycogen storage disease type II from deficient lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase, causing cardiomegaly, hypotonia and early heart failure.
Enlargement of the heart, seen on chest x-ray as a cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5.
Nitrogen bubbles forming in tissues after rapid ascent from diving, causing joint pain, neurologic deficits and respiratory symptoms.
Release of granule contents from cells such as mast cells, neutrophils and eosinophils.
A long-acting beta-2 agonist bronchodilator with fast onset, used in asthma and COPD together with an inhaled steroid.
An alpha-agonist decongestant that constricts nasal blood vessels. Can raise blood pressure and cause insomnia.
Excess albumin in urine, a marker of glomerular damage as in diabetic nephropathy.
A serum protein that blocks the complement C1 and bradykinin pathways. Deficiency causes hereditary angioedema.
A serine protease subunit of the C1 complex that cleaves C4 and C2 in the classical pathway.
Insufficient aldosterone, causing hyperkalemia, sodium loss and non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (type 4 renal tubular acidosis).
Acetylcholine-gated ion channels at autonomic ganglia, the neuromuscular junction and in the CNS. Blocked by curare and succinylcholine.
An inherited disease with cystic kidneys in infants, associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis and Potter sequence.
A group of disorders with fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys, including polycystic kidney disease and medullary sponge kidney.
A VHL tumor suppressor mutation causing retinal and cerebellar hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.
An abnormally large tongue, seen in hypothyroidism, Down syndrome, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and amyloidosis.
A phagocyte enzyme producing the respiratory burst of superoxide. Deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease.
A lipid of sphingosine and a fatty acid, the building block of sphingolipids. Accumulates in Gaucher and Fabry disease.
X-linked recessive mucopolysaccharidosis II from iduronate sulfatase deficiency. Features coarse face, aggressive behavior, no corneal clouding.
A liver enzyme that is raised in hepatocellular injury.
A urea cycle defect causing hyperammonemia without orotic aciduria.
A vitamin B12-dependent enzyme that converts homocysteine to methionine using methyltetrahydrofolate. Deficiency traps folate and causes megaloblastic anemia.
Dihydroxyphenylalanine, the intermediate made from tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase that is converted to dopamine. Levodopa is its drug form.
A purine salvage enzyme. Deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency through toxic buildup of lymphocyte deoxyadenosine.
A purine nucleoside of guanine and ribose.
The fish tapeworm acquired from raw freshwater fish, causing vitamin B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia.
Causes hemolytic anemia and neurologic disease with spinocerebellar degeneration and posterior column loss.
The system of macrophages in the liver, spleen, lymph nodes and bone marrow that clear particles and old red cells.
A heme synthesis intermediate that accumulates in urine in acute intermittent porphyria.
Paralysis of skeletal muscle by blocking acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, used in anesthesia.
Datura stramonium, a plant containing anticholinergic alkaloids. Poisoning causes mydriasis, dry skin, fever and delirium.
